channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The French government's 2027 draft finance bill, unveiled on 1 October, plans EUR 43 billion in recovery measures to reduce the public deficit to 5% of GDP in 2027, after a deficit the government says will widen to 5.5% this year.
item.description:
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had promised in mid-September a budget with EUR 54 billion in savings, Challenges reports. The draft projects growth of 1% in 2027, up from 0.5% in 2026, on a recovery in household consumption, and expects a further 0.3% fall in salaried employment, Les Echos reports. The government presents the budget without a majority to pass it, a few months before the presidential election; in the past two years France failed to adopt its finance law on time. Public debt has climbed to a record 119% of GDP and stood at EUR 3.596 trillion at the end of June, The Economic Times reports, and ECB President Christine Lagarde has called the debt situation "serious", Il Sole 24 Ore reports. French government bond yields climbed to a fresh 18-year high on 1 October, The Economic Times reports. The reporting does not give the split of the EUR 43 billion between spending cuts and revenue measures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The budget is a draft without a parliamentary majority, so both its measures and its deficit path remain uncertain. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, fiscal consolidation in a large euro-area economy tends to restrain public investment and household demand, and rising sovereign yields raise borrowing costs for French companies and construction projects. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, France is a large market for construction and industrial customers whose activity depends on public spending and credit conditions. Points that may be worth considering include which public investment and housing programmes the measures affect, and how French financing costs for customers and projects respond to yields at an 18-year high.

Challenges | Les Echos | The Financial Times | Les Echos | The Economic Times | Il Sole 24 Ore | The Economic Times

item.title: The US ISM manufacturing PMI fell to 54.5 in September from 54.6 in August, the ninth month of expansion, while its prices index rose 6.8 points to 77.9 from 71.1.
item.description:
The new orders index rose to 55.3 from 53.7 and the supplier deliveries index eased to 59.0 from 59.3, The Hindu Business Line reports, while MarketScreener reports that the supplier deliveries index slowed for a tenth consecutive month. The reading was below economists' expectations of 55 in a Reuters poll, Commercial Times reports, and of 54.9 in a Wall Street Journal poll, according to MarketScreener. S&P Global's final US manufacturing PMI rose to 55.9 from 53.9, its highest since May 2022 but revised down from a preliminary 57, Commercial Times reports. The Hindu Business Line says the jump in prices paid is consistent with economists' expectations that inflation could stay above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for some time. The reporting does not name which inputs drove the price increase.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The indices are purchasing-manager surveys: the headline shows a ninth month of expansion, and the prices index is a survey indicator, not a measured price change. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a prices index near 78 alongside slower supplier deliveries points to input-cost pressure across US manufacturing, which tends to show up in suppliers' price negotiations and in the Federal Reserve's view of inflation. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, US industrial customers facing higher input costs may push back on price increases while their own orders grow. Points that may be worth considering include which raw materials are driving US input prices, and how the price signal affects expectations for Federal Reserve policy.

MarketScreener | The Hindu Business Line - India | Commercial Times | MarketScreener

item.title: A document published by Cefic, the European chemical industry council, argues that the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement's battery rules should not be postponed again, after the carmakers' association ACEA called for their postponement.
item.description:
The rules require electric cars to use European batteries and cathodes to qualify for tariff-free trade between the EU and the UK, according to the document. It argues that the agreement created a commercial reason to buy European-made battery materials and build production in the EU and the UK, but that European carmakers were slow to back investment in the supply chain. At carmakers' request, the EU and UK agreed in December 2023 to postpone the rules by three years, with an explicit statement that no further postponement should be considered and restrictions on changing the rules before 2032. The document says Maroš Šefčovič, then a Commission Executive Vice-President and now Trade Commissioner, promised legal certainty and that companies were assured the extension was a one-off. The reporting does not say which groups stand behind the document, give the date the rules take effect, or report a Commission response.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The document is an advocacy position, not a decision; it sets the groups behind it against the carmakers on the same trade rule. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, rules of origin decide where battery materials must be made for vehicles to trade tariff-free, so keeping them supports investment in European cathode and cell production, while a postponement would favour cheaper imported batteries. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, battery assembly is an application for bonding, sealing and thermal-management materials, and where cells and modules are built shapes where those materials are bought. Points that may be worth considering include which European battery projects depend on the rules taking effect, and how a decision either way could change the location of battery assembly customers.

Cefic - The European Chemical Industry Council
item.source: Cefic - The European Chemical Industry Council

item.title: The US Commerce Department has slowed the approval of export licences for aircraft parts destined for China in recent weeks, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters, and is limiting the parts licensed for COMAC.
item.description:
Officials are also considering new rules that could make it easier to restrict shipments of landing gear and other aircraft components, and one of the sources said a proposed licensing requirement for aviation hydraulic fluid supplied by US companies such as ExxonMobil was included in a draft of the regulation, LiveMint reports. The number of parts licensed for shipment to COMAC, China's state-owned aircraft manufacturer, is being limited to prevent it from building up large inventories of US-made components, according to another source cited in the reports. The administration is seeking to turn China's dependence on US aviation suppliers into leverage in trade negotiations, Commercial Times reports; the paper adds that the US is trying to weaken China's control over rare earth minerals, and the sources say the department is ready to expand pressure on Beijing if the White House requests it. The reporting does not give the number of licences delayed, a timetable for the draft rule, or any official statement.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reports rest on anonymous sources and describe administrative practice and a draft rule, not a published measure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, export controls that reach aviation fluids and other consumables, not only finished parts, extend the scope of technology controls into chemical products, and China's response could reach the rare-earth supplies the US is seeking to secure. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, aerospace adhesives and sealants are qualified materials in the same supply chain, so a broadening of controls from components to fluids would be a broadening that reaches US-origin materials shipped to Chinese aircraft programmes. Points that may be worth considering include which US-origin aerospace materials are supplied to COMAC programmes, and whether the draft rule's scope is published.

LiveMint | Chinatimes.com | Commercial Times

item.title: EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen proposes postponing new EU rules to limit methane emissions by one year, with the EU reasoning that a later introduction would relieve pressure on energy markets and lower oil and gas prices.
item.description:
Jørgensen is under pressure from France and industry associations, Yahoo Germany reports. The report states that methane is responsible for around 30% of the increase in global temperatures since the Industrial Revolution and has contributed significantly to this summer's record heatwaves in Europe. The reporting does not specify which obligations would be postponed, whether they apply to EU producers or to importers of oil and gas, the original start date, or what procedure the postponement would need. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is a commissioner's proposal, not an adopted change. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, methane rules that require importers to show the emissions performance of their suppliers, if these rules include such obligations, can narrow the pool of eligible oil and gas sellers, so a postponement aims to keep more supply available to Europe during the current price shock. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the effect would be indirect, through gas and oil prices that reach energy costs and petrochemical raw materials. Points that may be worth considering include whether the postponement is adopted and for which obligations, and how it fits with any other EU steps to lower energy prices.

Yahoo! - Germany

item.title: Forvia plans to cut up to 10,000 jobs across Europe, and CEO Martin Fischer sees the automotive supply industry facing a historic upheaval, Frankfurter Rundschau reports, adding that small and medium-sized suppliers increasingly face existential threats.
item.description:
Forvia, formed from the merger of Faurecia and lighting specialist Hella, is the world's seventh-largest automotive supplier, Frankfurter Rundschau reports. The planned cuts cover all business areas and functions in Europe; in Germany the restructuring mainly affects the former Hella business. Former premium technologies such as LED headlights have become standardised mass-market products, and the company must re-earn its growth to remain profitable, the paper reports. Forvia sees growth in its electronics division (Hella Electronics) and in vehicle seats, and it intends to sell its Interiors division to reduce debt by EUR 1 billion. The reporting does not give the timing of the cuts, the split by country, the number of German jobs affected, or any count of supplier insolvencies supporting the warning. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The job cuts are a company plan and the warning about smaller suppliers is an assessment, not a measured count of insolvencies. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, when a large supplier restructures and sells divisions, ownership and sourcing decisions for whole product lines can change, and financial stress at smaller suppliers raises the risk of supply interruptions and unpaid receivables in the tiers below the carmakers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, interior and lighting components are applications for bonding and sealing materials, so a change of owner for Forvia's Interiors division could reopen material approvals. Points that may be worth considering include the credit exposure to smaller automotive suppliers in Europe, and how the Interiors sale may affect existing supply agreements.

Frankfurter Rundschau

item.title: The S&P Global final manufacturing PMI for Germany fell slightly to 53.9 in September from 54.3 in August, above the flash reading of 53.8, with new orders rising for a fourth month and input price inflation at its highest since June.
item.description:
Export sales grew again on demand from Asia, Europe and the US, MarketScreener reports. Cost pressures intensified in September after easing in the previous three months: input price inflation rose to its highest since June, and output price inflation edged up to a three-month high. The reporting does not give the output or employment sub-indices, a breakdown by industry, or the size of the changes in the price sub-indices. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The index is a survey of purchasing managers, not a measurement of production volume, and it shows new orders rising for a fourth month while cost pressures intensify. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, rising input prices alongside output prices only edging up suggest manufacturers are absorbing part of the input cost increase, which tends to put pressure on their suppliers' prices. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German industrial customers with growing orders and rising costs may combine higher volumes with stronger resistance to price increases. Points that may be worth considering include how German customers' order intake in September compares with this survey, and how far raw-material cost increases can be passed on if customers' own margins come under pressure.

MarketScreener

item.title: An earthen dyke breach flooded Phases 7 to 10 of Amata City Chonburi Industrial Estate in Thailand by 30–70 cm, and at least 34 factories sustained direct damage, The Nation reports.
item.description:
The Federation of Thai Industries' preliminary estimate puts direct losses from flooding across Bangkok and 14 provinces at USD 30.4 million, based on an assumed 40% impact rate among members in affected zones and covering equipment damage, raw material losses, supply chain halts and logistics disruption; repair teams are working to seal perimeter breaches, The Nation reports. In another report The Nation gives the FTI's provisional estimate of members' losses between 24 and 30 September as THB 1.02 billion; the FTI is still collecting damage reports, particularly from industrial estates in Chonburi, and will revise the estimate. Honda Motor and Toyota Motor halted some production, and the University of the Thai Chamber of Commerce estimates flooding in Bangkok and dozens of provinces could shave about 0.07 percentage point off economic growth, as much as THB 12.3 billion, and that damage could double if flooding persists, The Straits Times reports. The Bank of Thailand says initial effects are concentrated in services and the full economic impact cannot yet be assessed. The reporting does not name the damaged factories or their products, or say how long the carmakers' halts will last.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The loss figures are estimates, the FTI's preliminary, and are not additive; the factory damage is reported. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, Chonburi's industrial estates are a centre of Thailand's automotive and electrical manufacturing, so damage there reaches supply chains beyond the factories flooded, and production halts at carmakers tend to pass back to their component suppliers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, customers in Thai automotive and electronics assembly could postpone orders while sites are repaired, and deliveries into flooded estates may need rerouting. Points that may be worth considering include which customer and supplier sites are in the affected Amata City phases, how long carmakers' halts last, and whether the FTI's revised estimate changes the picture.

The Nation - Thailand | The Nation - Thailand | The Straits Times | The Nation - Thailand

item.title: US construction spending rose 0.9% in August from July to USD 2.20 trillion but was 1.7% below August 2025, the Associated General Contractors of America reports.
item.description:
Private residential construction rose 1.1% and private non-residential construction 1.0% in the month, AGC reports. Manufacturing construction was unchanged from July and 20% below its August 2025 level. Private "office" construction, which includes data centres, rose 4.6% from July and 30% year on year; data-centre construction alone rose 7.5% in the month and 73% over 12 months, while other private office construction was unchanged from July and 9.4% below a year earlier. The reporting does not give public construction spending, the split between new building and renovation, price-adjusted figures, or the size of the residential and non-residential segments. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The data are spending in dollars, not volumes, and the monthly rise sits on a level still below a year earlier. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, the split matters more than the total: data-centre construction is growing fast while manufacturing construction has fallen by a fifth, so demand for building materials is shifting between project types rather than rising across the board. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, data centres call for flooring, sealing, fire-protection and electronics-assembly materials, while weaker factory construction reduces demand in industrial building projects. Points that may be worth considering include how US construction customers' order books split between data-centre and other projects, and whether the 1.1% monthly rise in private residential construction continues.

Associated General Contractors of America

item.title: The share of recyclate in the plastic of PET beverage bottles in Germany was around 58% last year, about seven percentage points higher than in 2023, according to a GVM study commissioned by the plastics packaging association IK.
item.description:
The study by the Society for Packaging Market Research (GVM) was commissioned by the Industrievereinigung Kunststoffverpackungen (IK), the German association for plastics packaging and films, which evaluated the development positively, Handelsblatt and Wirtschaftswoche report. According to the IK, one reason for the increase is that companies aim to improve their carbon footprint. Wirtschaftswoche reports that the EU minimum requirement of 25% is significantly exceeded and that the tightening of the requirement to 30% planned for 2030 should also not be a problem for Germany. The reporting does not give the volume of PET bottles or recyclate, the share for other packaging types, the source of the recyclate (bottle-to-bottle or other streams), or the price of recyclate compared with virgin PET.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figure is a share of recycled material in one packaging type in one country, not a volume. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a high recyclate share in PET bottles depends on clean collection streams, which collection systems such as deposit schemes can support, and it raises the importance of how labels and their adhesives behave in washing and recycling processes. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, labelling adhesives that separate cleanly in bottle-to-bottle recycling are part of what makes a high recyclate share achievable. Points that may be worth considering include whether beverage customers in Germany and elsewhere are tightening specifications for label and closure materials as recyclate shares rise, and whether the EU's planned 30% requirement for 2030 leads to similar changes in other markets.

Handelsblatt | Wirtschafts Woche

item.title: Chinese refiners have suspended exports of oil products beyond Hong Kong and Macau until further notice, Reuters reported citing four people familiar with the matter, and the new front-month December Brent contract settled 4.37% higher at USD 102.31.
item.description:
Oil prices fell 1% early in the session and reversed after the Reuters report, Dawn reports; a Wall Street Journal report that the US was sending a third aircraft carrier and up to 10,000 more troops to the Middle East, as President Trump weighed resuming strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, contributed to a volatile session. US WTI settled 2.71% higher at USD 92.87. Separately, Russia this week extended its ban on diesel exports to the end of October, and President Putin said Russia will not supply diesel to global markets until sanctions are lifted, Valor Econômico reports. In the EU the average pump price of diesel has reached a new high of EUR 2.24 a litre, against EUR 1.59 before the outbreak of the war in the Middle East, according to the European Commission, Commercial Times reports. In Germany diesel has reached EUR 2.44 a litre. The reporting does not give the volumes of Chinese product exports affected, the products covered, the reason for the suspension, or any official Chinese confirmation.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The suspension is reported by anonymous sources and has not been officially confirmed in the reporting; the price move is measured. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, China has been a large exporter of refined products to Asian markets, so a halt shifts demand onto other refiners at a time when Russian diesel is also withheld, and refined-product prices tend to rise faster than crude when export capacity is withdrawn. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, diesel prices reach logistics costs directly, and a tighter refined-product market can also tighten naphtha and other refinery streams that feed petrochemical raw materials. Points that may be worth considering include how freight surcharges and raw-material price formulas respond to diesel at record levels, and which Asian supply routes depend on Chinese refined products.

Dawn | Valor Econômico | Commercial Times

item.title: Feique estimates that higher gas and electricity prices will add about EUR 1 billion to the Spanish chemical sector's energy bills from the start of the conflict to the end of the year, putting the continuity of multiple plants at risk.
item.description:
Feique, the Spanish chemical industry federation, informed a broad representation of the Ministries of Economy and Industry, headed by First Vice-President and Minister of Economy, Trade and Business Carlos Cuerpo and Minister of Industry and Tourism Jordi Hereu, about the critical situation that the rise in natural gas and electricity prices is creating for the sector, according to Feique. The EUR 1 billion is an estimate based on forecasts in energy futures markets and covers the period from the beginning of the conflict until the end of the year. The reporting does not say whether Feique asked the government for specific measures, or which plants or product segments are most at risk, how the estimate compares with the sector's normal energy bill, or how the government responded. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figure is a sector association's estimate of additional cost, based on forecasts in energy futures markets, not a measurement of output or of closures. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, energy-intensive basic chemistry is usually the first part of a chemical industry to cut runs when gas and power prices rise, and Spanish producers compete in the same European market as producers in countries with different energy-price support. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Spanish chemical plants are part of the European supply base for raw materials, so curtailments there would show up first as tighter availability or higher prices for intermediates. Points that may be worth considering include which raw materials sourced from Spanish producers carry the most energy cost, and whether the Spanish government responds with support for energy-intensive chemicals, and how any such support would compare across EU states.

FEIQUE - Federación Empresarial de la Industria Química Española
item.source: FEIQUE - Federación Empresarial de la Industria Química Española
